The cleanest answer is:

> **Poissonian micro-absorption with rare-event thinning.**

That is the detector physics I would trust most.

## Core idea

Suppose absorbed power (P) is not treated as a smooth fluid, but as a stream of microscopic absorption opportunities.

If each microscopic absorption event carries characteristic energy (\varepsilon), then the arrival rate of such events is

$$
r(P) \approx \frac{P}{\varepsilon}.
$$

Now assume each event has a small, approximately power-independent probability (p_{\text{trig}}) of launching the irreversible detector nucleation.

Then the nucleation rate is just the thinned Poisson rate:

$$
\lambda(P) \approx p_{\text{trig}},r(P)
= \frac{p_{\text{trig}}}{\varepsilon},P.
$$

So

$$
\boxed{\lambda(P)\approx \alpha P,\qquad \alpha=\frac{p_{\text{trig}}}{\varepsilon}.}
$$

That is the least circular route I see.

## Why this is not “smuggling Born in”

Because the square law is **not** coming from the detector.

It comes earlier:

1. **Linear analyzer projection**
   $$
   c_i = u_i^\dagger a
   $$

2. **Absorbed branch power is quadratic in amplitude**
   $$
   P_i \propto |c_i|^2
   $$

3. **Detector rate is linear in absorbed power**
   $$
   \lambda_i \propto P_i
   $$

Therefore

$$
\lambda_i \propto |c_i|^2.
$$

So the detector is only contributing the **linear-in-power** step. The square already came from ordinary linear-wave + quadratic-energy physics.

That is much better than just postulating
$$
\lambda_i \propto |c_i|^2
$$
directly.

## What physical detector class does this correspond to?

A detector with:

* many microscopic absorption attempts,
* each attempt independent,
* each attempt individually unlikely to trigger,
* first successful trigger launches avalanche/latch.

That is the regime.

## Concrete physics pictures

### 1. Weakly efficient avalanche detector

Each absorbed carrier or hot carrier has small chance to seed avalanche.

If carrier creation rate is proportional to absorbed power, and avalanche probability per carrier is roughly constant, then
$$
\lambda \propto P.
$$

This is probably the best engineering candidate.

### 2. Metastable latch with rare trigger quanta

Absorbed power creates random microscopic excitations at rate (P/\varepsilon). Each excitation perturbs a near-threshold latch. If the latch is biased so each excitation has small fixed success probability, again:
$$
\lambda \propto P.
$$

### 3. Shot-noise absorber

If the branch absorber naturally sees discrete arrival events whose mean rate is proportional to local intensity/power, and the detector commits on the first successful one, same result.

This is basically the abstract detector theorem in physical language.

## What conditions are required?

For the linear law to hold over a usable range, you need:

### A. Independent micro-events

The absorption opportunities should look approximately Poissonian.

### B. Rare-trigger regime

Each event should have
$$
p_{\text{trig}} \ll 1
$$
so triggers are rare and independent.

### C. Constant per-event trigger probability

Over the operating range, (p_{\text{trig}}) should not vary much with power.

If (p_{\text{trig}}) grows strongly with power, you get curvature.

### D. No long integration memory

The detector should not need to accumulate many events before deciding.

That was exactly what broke the earlier accumulator models.

### E. Fast latch after first trigger

Once one event succeeds, the detector must latch quickly enough to suppress competitors.

## What physics would *not* give the law cleanly?

### Deterministic threshold crossing

This gives “bigger branch almost always wins.”

### Many-event accumulation

Same problem.

### Strongly exponential escape

For example,
$$
\lambda(P)\sim e^{\beta P}
$$
unless you operate in a tiny linearized regime.

### Thermal integration detectors

Usually too much memory, unless run in a very special metastable rare-event mode.

## Best engineering statement

The detector physics you want is:

> **branch absorbed power creates a Poisson stream of microscopic trigger opportunities, and each opportunity has a small approximately constant chance of launching the detector’s irreversible nucleation.**

Then

$$
\lambda(P)\approx \alpha P
$$

falls out naturally.

## Why this is the strongest answer

Because it gives you an actual mechanism chain:

$$
P \rightarrow \text{micro-event rate} \rightarrow \text{rare successful trigger} \rightarrow \lambda
$$

instead of just assuming the answer.

## The real experimental question

The right next test is not “does the theory sound nice?”

It is:

> **Can we build or identify a detector cell whose measured click rate is linear in absorbed branch power over a calibrated range, while staying in the rare-event regime?**

That is the key hardware question now.

## The one-line version

$$
\boxed{\text{Use a rare-event avalanche/latch detector where microscopic absorption events arrive at rate }P/\varepsilon\text{ and each has small fixed success probability.}}
$$

That is the cleanest known route to
$$
\lambda(P)\approx \alpha P
$$
without just inserting Born by hand.
